extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students studying introductory combinatorics / proof
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter introducing fundamental counting techniques (Pascal's triangle, binomial theorem, inclusion–exclusion, multisets and stars-and-bars, division/pigeonhole). Includes definitions, core facts, formulas, and worked examples for solving elementary combinatorial counting problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's triangle recurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any number (other than 1) in Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two numbers immediately above it; equivalently C(n+1,k) = C(n,k-1) + C(n,k) for 0 < k < n+1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct new rows by placing 1 at each end and obtaining each interior entry by adding the two entries above. Example: 21 is the sum of 6 and 15 above it. This recurrence is the combinatorial identity used to build the triangle and derive other identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pascal's triangle symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The kth entry of Row n equals the (n−k)th entry: C(n,k) = C(n,n−k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pascal's triangle is symmetric about its vertical axis (Row 0 at top). Use this symmetry to simplify computations and reason about binomial coefficients (e.g., only need compute up to floor(n/2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: For non-negative integer n, (x + y)^n = sum_{k=0}^n C(n,k) x^{n-k} y^k (Theorem 3.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Row n of Pascal's triangle lists the coefficients of (x+y)^n. Use the theorem to expand powers of binomials (examples: (x+y)^7 expanded using Row 7; (2a−b)^4 expanded with appropriate powers and signs). The textbook defers proof to exercises but emphasizes practical use for expansions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binomial coefficient formula
rubrics_metrics.description: C(n,k) = n! / (k!(n−k)!) for 0 ≤ k ≤ n (definition/standard formula for 'n choose k').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this closed form to compute entries of Pascal's triangle (e.g., entries in Row 8 are C(8,k)). Also used in algebraic expansions via the binomial theorem and in combinatorial counting arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of binomial coefficients (row sum)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This identity follows from evaluating (1+1)^n. Useful for counting subsets or total counts across all k; used in exercises and examples to simplify totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion–exclusion for two sets
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are finite sets then |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| (Fact 3.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: counting A and B separately double-counts the intersection, so subtract |A ∩ B|. Use to reduce union-count problems to counts of components. Special case: if A ∩ B = ∅ then |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| (addition principle). Example: counting 3-card hands that are all red or all face cards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion–exclusion for three sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For sets A, B, C: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |A ∩ C| − |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension of two-set formula: add single counts, subtract pairwise intersections (over-counted twice), then add back triple intersection (subtracted three times). Useful for more complex union-count problems; presented with Venn diagram guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction principle (complement counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count objects not having a property, compute total count minus count with the property (used in Example 3.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model: number of outcomes that do not satisfy predicate P = total outcomes − number that do satisfy P. Useful when complement is easier to count. Example: number of 3-card hands that are not (all red or all face cards) = total 3-card hands − number that are all red or all face cards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stars-and-bars encoding for multisets
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode a k-element multiset chosen from an n-element set as a list of k stars and n−1 bars, with bars separating counts for each element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each multiset corresponds to a string with k '*' symbols and n−1 '|' separators; conversely any such string encodes a multiset. Examples: encoding 5-element multisets from {a,b,c,d} as 5 stars and 3 bars (length 8). This concrete encoding leads directly to binomial counts by choosing positions for bars (or stars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of k-element multisets from n elements (Fact 3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of k-element multisets from an n-element set X is C(k+n−1, k) = C(k+n−1, n−1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from stars-and-bars: choose n−1 positions out of k+n−1 for bars (or k positions for stars). Use for counting outcomes with repetition allowed (examples: distributions of identical marbles, multisets of letters). Examples: 20-element multisets from 3 colors → C(22,20)=231.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting nonnegative integer solutions via stars-and-bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of nonnegative integer solutions to x1 + x2 + ... + xn = k equals C(k+n−1, n−1) (equivalence to k-element multisets from an n-element set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model each variable's value as the number of stars before a separating bar. Example: solutions to w+x+y+z = 20 correspond to 20 stars and 3 bars → C(23,3)=1771. Use either multiset viewpoint or explicit bar-position counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutations of a multiset (Fact 3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a multiset has n total elements with multiplicities p1, p2, ..., pk then number of distinct permutations = n! / (p1! p2! ... pk!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model distinct labeled objects first (n!) then divide by factorials for indistinguishable repeats. Examples: BOOK → 4!/2! = 12; BANANA → 6!/(3!2!) = 60; MISSISSIPPI calculation shown. Use this for counting distinct arrangements when items repeat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division principle (average / floor & ceiling form, Fact 3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n objects are placed into k boxes then at least one box contains ceil(n/k) or more objects, and at least one box contains floor(n/k) or fewer objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning via average objects per box. Use floor/ceiling to derive guaranteed lower/upper bounds on occupancy. This is the 'strong form' used to reason about guarantees (e.g., in 100 people some month has at least ceil(100/12) people born).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (Fact 3.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n objects are placed into k boxes and n > k then at least one box contains more than one object; if n < k then at least one box is empty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A direct corollary of the division principle. Widely used in existence/guarantee proofs. Examples: among 13 people at least two share a birth month; picking 6 numbers from 0..9 forces two that sum to 9 by pairing boxes; gumball problem uses ceil(n/4)≥13 to deduce minimal purchase of 49.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling technique: view counting problems as placing objects into boxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many combinatorial problems are solved by modeling choices as objects (stars, items, people) placed into boxes (categories, bins, variable slots), then applying counting principles (choose positions for bars/stars, inclusion-exclusion, division/pigeonhole, subtraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text repeatedly illustrates modeling choices (cards, marbles, digits, coins, letters) into boxes and then applying an appropriate principle (addition, multiplication, subtraction, inclusion–exclusion, stars-and-bars, division/pigeonhole). Recognize which principle fits the model before computing binomial coefficients or factorial ratios.
